2610.40766.abstract: An analysis of 29 quadruply imaged quasars hints at dark matter halo densities consistent with gravothermal core collapse, a key prediction of self-interacting dark matter. We interpret this evidence through elastic Yukawa scattering, combining lensing with upper limits on the cross-section strength from galaxy clusters and Milky Way satellite evaporation. Favored models have dark matter masses of $20$-$80\,{\rm GeV}$, MeV-scale mediators, and Yukawa-potential strengths near $10^{-3}$, yielding cross-sections of $10^2$--$10^4 \, {\rm cm^2\,g^{-1}}$ at $10\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$. Cosmological, direct and indirect detection bounds on MeV-scale mediators motivate a neutrinophilic scalar dilepton that decays invisibly without Higgs mixing. These results demonstrate how inferences on core collapse constrain dark sector physics.

2610.40770.abstract: As observations of the cosmic dawn (CD) and epoch of reionisation (EoR) rapidly improve in precision, the approximate forward models used to interpret them might struggle to keep pace. Bayesian inference with a misspecified model, one that cannot represent the processes generating the observations, can yield tightly constrained, yet misleading and biased astrophysics, with different parts of the observations favouring incompatible parameter values. Model misspecification can evade a $\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit test, and Bayesian model selection requires a better model, which is not always available. We therefore apply the suspiciousness, a statistic developed to quantify tensions between datasets, to CD/EoR inference as a model criticism tool that tests whether these parts can be explained by the same parameters. We first apply it to HERA 21-cm power spectrum (PS) upper limits, which are too weak to reveal misspecification, as expected, and to HST and JWST UV luminosity functions (LFs). Under our galaxy model, the UV LFs at $z\leq10$ and $z>10$ are in tension at $5.0\sigma$ in the Gaussian limit, a failure visible in the fits, although doubling the uncertainties of the $z>10$ observations reduces it to $2.1\sigma$. Finally, we analyse a mock SKA-Low AA$^\ast$ 1080 h 21-cm PS with the model that generated it and with a simpler, misspecified model. We find that the misspecified model silently fails: it fits the PS well, passing visual inspection and, for most noise realisations, a $\chi^2$ test, yet its inferred astrophysics is wrong. The Bayesian evidence disfavours it, but only relative to the true model, which is unavailable for real observations. The suspiciousness finds no tension for the well-specified model, but a $\sim3.4\sigma$ tension for the misspecified one, strongly ruling it out without requiring a more adequate candidate model.

2610.40785.abstract: While there is ample evidence that the universe's expansion is accelerating, most of this evidence relies on assuming a shape of the relative expansion rate, $H(z)/H_0$, informed by a cosmological model or a kinematical approach. Model-independent analyses are common for supernova datasets but rarely applied to other data. In this work, we use uncalibrated baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) from DESI DR2 for a model-independent test of acceleration, which makes no assumptions about the theory of gravity or the energy content of the universe. We test for cosmic acceleration with three model-independent statistics that rely purely on the measured Alcock-Paczyński parameter, the isotropic BAO, and the line-of-sight BAO, and do not require any reconstruction between redshift bins unlike previous analyses. Accounting for the look-elsewhere effect, among all statistics we find $2.4\sigma$ - $4.1\sigma$ evidence for cosmic acceleration within $0 \leq z \leq 0.934$ when assuming flatness; allowing for spatial curvature, $|\Omega_k| \leq 1$, at least two of the three statistics retain $2.4\sigma$ - $3.5\sigma$.

2610.40846.abstract: We develop a continuous framework connecting quantum field fluctuations in the early Universe to the abundance and observable properties of galaxies and active galactic nuclei (AGN) at cosmic dawn. Beginning with quantum fields in curved Friedmann Lemaitre Robertson Walker spacetime, we follow inflationary vacuum fluctuations into the primordial curvature spectrum, linear matter power spectrum, mass variance $\sigma(MHz)$, mass peak height $u(MHz)$, and the statistics of nonlinear halo formation. The Press-Schechter and Sheth-Tormen formalisms provide an analytic description of halo abundance and its dependence on peak rarity. A complementary high redshift halo mass function calibrated with the GUREFT simulations of Yung et al. (2024) provides a numerical description specifically constructed for the cosmic dawn regime probed by JWST. The comparison between these analytic and simulation calibrated prescriptions provides a direct measure of the sensitivity of predicted halo populations to the observations. We separate this cosmological supply of halos from the astrophysical and observational mappings that produce stars, ultraviolet luminosities, and active galactic nuclei. Controlled numerical experiments show that a percent level perturbation in the primordial fluctuation amplitude produces only a modest change in $\sigma$ and $u$, but can strongly amplify the exponentially suppressed high $u$ tail of the Halo Mass Function. This sensitivity increases toward high halo mass and high redshift, identifying rare cosmic dawn populations as potentially powerful probes of primordial statistics while simultaneously exposing the importance of uncertainties in halo abundance. High redshift AGN population statistics and the Ultraviolet Luminosity Function provide additional constraints on the primordial power spectrum and dynamics of primordial inflation theory.

2610.40875.abstract:
We present FOMO-Z (Flexible Optimizer of Multi-dimensional Operators and photo-$z$s), a set of statistical methods implemented in Python for galaxy classification and probabilistic inference from photometry.
The methods use a reference sample with known galaxy properties. They rely on explicit, physically interpretable criteria and make no assumptions about the functional form of the color distributions. Binary selections are calibrated using either linear color conditions, particularly suited to background galaxy selection, or flexible color--color grids, seeking to maximize completeness given a threshold on purity. For probabilistic inference, the code identifies reference objects with compatible colors within photometric uncertainties to estimate each test galaxy's probability of satisfying user-defined criteria, as well as probability density functions of continuous properties such as redshift. The code also reconstructs property distributions of selected galaxy populations using photometrically similar galaxies in the reference sample. This framework supports prior weights and reference redshift probability distributions. A built-in feature-selection method identifying informative colors is also introduced.
We demonstrate applications to background galaxy selection, galaxy population classification, tomographic redshift calibration, and photometric redshift estimation. The code achieves results consistent with those obtained through machine-learning approaches, such as self-organizing maps, while remaining computationally efficient, making it suitable for large photometric surveys and future Stage IV cosmological analyses. The code is publicly available at this https URL.

2610.41077.abstract: We show that the vacuum metamorphosis model with decay fits current baryon acoustic oscillation and supernova distance data and cosmic microwave background measurements significantly better than $\Lambda$CDM and nearly as well as $w_0w_a$CDM with the same number of parameters. Vacuum metamorphosis with decay provides a physically motivated model of dark energy and an explanation of current cosmological data. In this scenario, non-perturbative quantum effects of a massive scalar field freeze the Ricci scalar curvature when it reaches a critical value proportional to the mass squared, inducing a phase transition in the scalar field, giving a phantom dark energy equation of state $w<-1$. After the phase transition, vacuum energy decays into light particles, providing a natural mechanism for the dark-energy equation of state to cross the phantom divide from $w<-1$ to $w>-1$, in agreement with current cosmological indications, without requiring an explicit coupling to matter.

2610.41252.abstract: Ground-based millimeter and submillimeter telescopes produce astronomical maps that contain a combination of noise inherent to themselves as well as contamination from foregrounds, with the strongest foreground being fluctuating atmospheric emission. While the emission of the turbulent atmosphere itself follows a scale-free power law, the atmosphere as seen by the telescope is modified by the properties of the instrument optics. A naive power-law extrapolation of the atmospheric noise spectrum ignores the blurring effect of the near-field beam, which becomes more pronounced for larger telescope apertures and at higher multipoles. In this work, we use a toy model to derive a semianalytic estimate of the atmospheric noise spectrum that takes into account the effects of near-field optics. We show that it has an appreciable effect for large-aperture telescopes, suggesting that ultra-sensitive, high-resolution experiments are not necessarily limited by the atmosphere on small angular scales. We also present an estimate of the atmospheric knee as a function of the primary aperture, the atmospheric scale height, and the outer scale of turbulence.

2610.41796.abstract: We present a new rescaling and stacking method to test cold dark matter predictions through the dynamical modelling of galaxy groups using the Jeans equation. We test the viability of this method on idealised, line-of-sight group data at $z=0$ in the IllustrisTNG-300 simulation, using subhalos and satellite galaxies as tracers. Dynamical mass profiles are measured using the code `Gravsphere' for seven distinct quality cuts, three on the dark matter substructure and four on the `visible' satellite galaxies. When using the dark matter substructure, we find that selecting subhalos by their infall time onto the group provides the best recovery of the true mass profile. When using satellite galaxies we instead find that selecting quenched satellites provides the best recovery. In both cases the mass profile is recovered within $<1\sigma$ of the true value up to $\sim 1.5$ times the median host virial radius. However, we also find the recovered velocity anisotropy to be biased towards negative values for all seven of our subhalo samples beyond the median host virial radius. This suggests dynamical systematics may still be present in the data, which will need to be quantified in future work before application to surveys.

2610.41823.abstract: We study the production of primordial black holes (PBHs) and scalar-induced gravitational waves (SIGWs) in aligned axion inflation through the transition between two stages of inflation. The first stage proceeds along a metastable trajectory and ends when this trajectory loses stability, causing the fields to turn towards the attractor of the second inflationary stage. During the transition, coupled adiabatic--entropy evolution produces a localized enhancement of the curvature power spectrum. We compute the PBH abundance from this spectrum assuming Gaussian primordial curvature perturbations and using the nonlinear compaction-function formalism with a spectrum-dependent collapse threshold and critical collapse. Representative benchmark solutions yield asteroid-mass PBHs with a potentially significant dark-matter abundance, together with an associated SIGW background.

2610.41914.abstract: We present a fast and accurate method for computing the two-loop matter power spectrum in the Effective Field Theory of Large-Scale Structure (EFTofLSS). Using FFTLog, we decompose the linear power spectrum into complex power laws, reducing the two-loop corrections to cosmology-independent massless Feynman integrals of kite topology. A central numerical challenge is the evaluation of these integrals for complex powers with large imaginary parts, where the highly oscillatory integrands make accurate numerical evaluation particularly challenging. We overcome this difficulty using a Mellin--Barnes representation summed over a uniform lattice, achieving approximately ten digit precision even for large imaginary powers, with an error estimate for each integral. The resulting precomputed matrices allow the two-loop power spectrum to be evaluated for a new cosmology in a few milliseconds. Comparing with direct numerical integration, we find agreement at the $10^{-4}$ level relative to the power spectrum up to $k=0.2$ $h$Mpc$^{-1}$ after accounting for EFTofLSS counterterm contributions and FFTLog decomposition errors. The same framework extends to biased tracers and redshift-space distortions, providing the building blocks for general two-loop calculations in EFTofLSS. We make the code for evaluating the kite integrals publicly available, together with precomputed matrices and an implementation for the two-loop matter power spectrum as a concrete application. Our results can be directly incorporated into existing FFTLog-based codes for large-scale structure, extending their current one-loop capabilities to two loops within the same computational framework.

2610.41940.abstract: The technique of 21 cm intensity mapping (IM) is emerging as a possible, cost-effective method to supplement optical surveys to map the large-scale structure, and extend their redshift reach, with projects aiming to cover a large range of post-EoR redshifts, from z=0 to z=6. Since the early discussions 20 years ago, a few dedicated interferometers have been built, and surveys have been carried out using them as well as general purpose radio instruments. An introduction to late-time cosmology with 21 cm intensity mapping is given, highlighting the main scientific and technical challenges. We present then an overview of different instrument concepts and survey strategies, followed by a discussion of outstanding data analysis challenges, most notably the foreground subtraction, which is a major issue in IM. We carry on with a presentation of the currently active projects and the 21 cm signal measurements which have been obtained, either in cross-correlation with optical surveys, or as the autocorrelation power spectrum. Finally, we discuss briefly the prospects for this field with future instruments and surveys such as SKA, HIRAX and CHORD.

2610.42044.abstract: In the context of stochastic inflation, specifying boundary conditions is often a requirement to distinguish domains where quantum diffusion takes place from regions where stochastic effects are suppressed compared to the standard slow-roll evolution. Yet, even though the transition between the two is expected to be smooth and continuous, most of the literature has hitherto focused on absorbing and reflective boundaries. We consider here the use of a broader class of boundaries, called elastic, which involves one free parameter interpolating between these two limiting cases. We show how the conventional stochastic-$\delta N$, and its recently proposed time-reversed counterpart adapt to such a class of boundary behaviour. As an illustration, we solve time-reversed stochastic inflation for an exactly flat semi-infinite potential with an elastic boundary, a setup where the standard stochastic-$\delta N$ formalism breaks down, and compare the results to the purely absorbing case. Quantitative differences are found in terms of skewness and tail behaviour. This suggests that the transition between stochastic inflation and subsequent evolution may have observable consequences. Finally, we show that an elastic boundary stands as an effective model for stochastic tunnelling through a Dirac delta potential barrier. This mechanism can be equivalently framed as a smooth transition of stochastic trajectories in a mirror virtual medium with specific absorption properties.

2610.42056.abstract: Recent work has shown that a simple form of coupled dark energy with a constant coupling produces a good fit to the DESI data. In this scenario, dark matter, but not baryons, couples to a scalar field, thereby violating the weak equivalence principle (EP). We first generalize the coupled dark energy model by adding a nonminimal coupling between the scalar field and gravity, and dub the resulting model "doubly coupled dark energy". We then construct a parameter $E_P$ in this model that quantifies EP violation on cosmological scales and can be measured with large galaxy surveys in a model-independent way. Finally, we forecast constraints on the couplings for present and future spectroscopic galaxy surveys, namely DESI, Euclid, and SKA Phase 2 (SKA2). To keep the analysis as general as possible, we leave the initial power spectrum shape and the galaxy bias free to vary in several bins. Among these surveys, SKA2 could provide the tightest constraint on the coupling strength in the coupled dark energy scenario, with a relative $1\sigma$ uncertainty of $22\%$. The constraints weaken when both couplings are varied, but can be further improved by increasing the number of galaxies detected.

2610.42151.abstract: Intrinsic alignments (IA) of galaxies are an important source of systematic uncertainty in weak gravitational lensing measurements and also serve as a test for models of galaxy formation and evolution. These galaxy alignments are usually modeled assuming that the IA are sourced by the tidal fields around the galaxies. However, galaxy properties, like their proximity to other galaxies and their mass, provide alignment contributions beyond the tidal field. In this work, we perform novel model-agnostic tests to determine the impact of density-weighting on the IA of galaxies using data from the IllustrisTNG cosmological hydrodynamical simulation and SDSS-III (BOSS). We show that the primary effect of density-weighting is an increase of the alignment amplitude at large scales, whereas the small-scale impact is sample-dependent. We also assess the tidal alignment paradigm for IllustrisTNG galaxies using two-point correlation functions of galaxy shapes, tidal fields, and the sampled background tidal field of the simulation box. We find, given the precision of our measurements, that central galaxies align linearly to the underlying (non-linear) tidal field well into the 1-halo regime.

2610.40354.abstract: We study the gravitational wave (GW) spectrum generated by supercooled first-order phase transitions in two-field conformal models. We construct three representative toy models that capture the essential features of these models, derive analytical criteria for the existence of two-step transitions, and show how the two-field dynamics generate a genuine two-peak GW spectrum. We identify regions of parameter space in which two-peak GW spectra are observable at LISA and the Einstein Telescope. By way of illustration, we apply our analysis to a realistic conformal dark SU(3) model.

2610.40781.abstract: First-order phase transitions in a dark sector can produce an observable stochastic gravitational-wave background, and many models predicting such signals in current and future experiments have been explored. For moderately strong transitions, hydrodynamical simulations suggest that sound waves generated by the expansion and collisions of true-vacuum bubbles are the dominant source of gravitational waves. It is often assumed that these sound waves propagate only within the dark-sector fluid, while the impact of the visible sector is neglected. In this paper, we investigate the effects of a weak coupling between the dark and visible fluids on the resulting gravitational-wave signal. We adopt a phenomenological hydrodynamical description of two ultra-relativistic fluids, parametrizing their interactions without specifying an underlying microscopic model. We focus on the regime in which the coupling can be neglected during the phase transition but becomes relevant during the subsequent, longer-lasting period of sound wave propagation. Within this framework, we analytically show that, even if the bubble expansion initially affects only the dark fluid, sound waves can subsequently be induced in the visible sector. Using the sound-shell model, we find that, despite the additional sound waves generated in the visible sector, the total gravitational-wave signal sourced by both fluids is generally suppressed compared to the case of a completely decoupled dark sector. This suppression becomes more pronounced for larger interaction rates and a larger ratio of relativistic degrees of freedom in the visible sector to those in the dark sector. The coupling also modifies the shape of the gravitational-wave spectrum.

2610.40787.abstract: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) disks are promising sites for hierarchical binary black hole (BBH) mergers, which next-generation gravitational-wave detectors will probe out to high redshift. Predicting their contribution requires linking BBH evolution in AGN disks to the poorly constrained high-redshift evolution of active supermassive black holes (SMBHs). We introduce ARISE (AGN Rates and Intrinsic Stellar-BH Evolution), a framework that embeds semi-analytical models of BBH evolution in AGN disks into a cosmological description of the AGN number density, SMBH mass function, Eddington-ratio distribution, and nuclear metallicity. We consider a conservative AGN-abundance model anchored to observed luminosity functions, as well as Eddington-limited and super-Eddington scenarios based on the CAT cosmological model, compatible with JWST observations of high-redshift AGNs. The merger-rate density is set primarily by the disk viscosity parameter $\alpha$: at $z = 0.2$, we find a rate of $12$--$37$ Gpc$^{-3}$ yr$^{-1}$ for $\alpha = 0.01$ and $0.5$--$6$ Gpc$^{-3}$ yr$^{-1}$ for $\alpha = 0.1$. The redshift evolution depends strongly on how SMBHs grow. The rate density peaks at $z \simeq 1.8$, $3.3$, and $3.9$ ($1.5$, $3.6$, and $3.9$) for $\alpha=0.01$ ($0.1$) in the conservative, Eddington-limited, and super-Eddington models, respectively, and in the super-Eddington model it stays nearly flat out to $z \simeq 10$. For $\alpha = 0.1$, AGN disks account for $\sim 2$--$40\%$ of the LVK-inferred merger rate, consistent with current upper limits from GW--AGN associations. For $\alpha = 0.01$, they match or exceed it. The Einstein Telescope (ET) should detect $\sim 10^{5}$ ($\sim 10^{4}$) AGN-disk mergers per year for $\alpha = 0.01$ ($0.1$). ET will test the AGN channel at redshifts where the AGN population models differ most strongly, providing independent constraints on the growth of early SMBHs.

2610.41491.abstract: We employ JWST/NIRSpec MSA PRISM spectroscopy together with NIRCam imaging to investigate the impact of star-formation variability on galaxy sizes for a representative sample of 51 galaxies at $z\geq4$. The OASIS survey enables us to probe low-star-formation-rate (SFR) lulling and mini-quenched galaxies down to $\log_{10}(M_\star/M_\odot)=8.3$ and $\log_{10}(\mathrm{SFR}/M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1})<-1.6$, i.e. more than one order of magnitude below the star-forming main sequence (MS). This enables us to probe objects that are often missed by shallower spectroscopic surveys, in addition to the MS and starburst systems, yielding an SFR- and mass-representative sample at high redshift. We derive galaxy half-light sizes using ForcePho, enabling us to resolve the highly compact nature of these sources, and we analyse their star-formation histories and interstellar medium (ISM) properties with the full-spectral-fitting code ppxf. We find a clear anti-correlation between burstiness, as traced by the ratio of the SFR from H$\alpha$ compared to that from non-parametric spectral fitting averaged over 100 Myr, and galaxy UV/optical half-light radii as measured with ForcePho from a combination of well-sampled NIRCam photometry. Using partial correlation coefficients we show that the anti-correlation between burstiness (as traced by the SFR ratio) and size cannot simply be explained by secondary dependencies on stellar mass or redshift. We interpret this relation as the effect of central starbursts in SFR-rising (bursting) systems, where intense central star formation reduces measured galaxy half-light sizes. This burstiness then regulates galaxy sizes at high redshift. Should the same mechanism be present at $z>10$, this could explain the size bimodality seen in the UV luminous galaxies as simply stemming from a more fundamental relationship between burstiness and size.

2610.41780.abstract: Thermogravity offers a novel approach to cosmic acceleration, deriving trace-free gravitational equations and matter non-conservation from thermodynamic processes in spacetime. We extend this framework towards thermocosmology by introducing a running non-conservation scale $L_2(H)$, while restricting non-conservation to cold dark matter. We investigate two prescriptions, namely a Hubble-proportional rate and an inverse-Hubble running model, deriving their cosmological dynamics and effective geometric dark-energy description. The first admits an exact analytical solution and is related to quadratic running-vacuum cosmologies, while the second approaches standard matter dilution at early times and allows reversals in the direction of energy exchange. Interestingly, the reconstructed geometric dark energy can exhibit quintessence-like and phantom-like behavior, including smooth crossings of the phantom divide, without introducing a phantom field or superacceleration. A unified dynamical-system analysis reveals distinct matter-era critical configurations and a continuous family of de Sitter solutions that are transversely attracting under suitable conditions. Confronting both models with Pantheon+ Type Ia supernovae, cosmic chronometers, and DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations, we find a mild preference for positive present-day matter non-conservation. The Akaike information criterion slightly favors the thermogravity scenarios, whereas the Bayesian information criterion favors the simpler $\Lambda$CDM model. Thus, running thermocosmology provides a viable framework for nontrivial effective dark-energy dynamics.

2610.41953.abstract: We investigate topological inflation in minimal multi-natural inflation, in which the axion potential consists of two cosine terms. Focusing on the high-scale regime, we perform a systematic parameter scan for representative ratios of the two periods and identify regions consistent with current constraints on the scalar spectral index and tensor-to-scalar ratio, including those from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. The interplay of the two harmonics allows departures from the quartic hilltop limit and accommodates the higher spectral index favored by recent cosmological data combinations. We characterize the hilltop and near-inflection-point branches and analyze the associated vacuum structure and domain-wall properties. We also discuss a symmetry-breaking origin of the required domain walls when the inflaton is the angular component of a complex scalar field. We identify regions in which the observational constraints and the adopted criteria for topological inflation are simultaneously satisfied, including regions with a sub-Planckian axion decay constant. Our results show that the observational tension encountered in the minimal quartic double-well model need not extend to topological inflation in a minimal multi-natural axion potential.
